clue.text: Handsome young man said: "No problem!"

indicators.note: something said is spoken, so the phrase that follows is judged by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a cheery reply meaning the matter is settled, a done issue, said quickly

explanation.surface: A good-looking lad is quoted giving a breezy reassurance.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound-alike is loose: 'No problem!' is read as 'a done is(sue)', said quickly enough to sound like ADONIS.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Adonis was a youth of great beauty, so his name is used for any handsome young man.

clue.text: Much too high a price to pay in exchange for "Gilt Hero" by Brady

definitions.text: Much too high a price to pay

indicators.note: an exchange swaps things about, so the quoted words have their letters traded around

parts.note: taken letter for letter, including the word by

explanation.surface: Someone pays far too much to swap for a painting or book called Gilt Hero by an artist named Brady.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'by' looks like an attribution but its letters are part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Daylight robbery is the idiom for a blatant overcharge, a price so steep it feels like theft.

clue.text: Nick's back on time with honour

indicators.note: going back means reading the short word that follows from its end to its start

parts.note: taken as written
T is the standard abbreviation for time
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick is back promptly, carrying an honour.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a man's name, but it is the definition, a small cut. CH (Companion of Honour) is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A nick and a notch are both small V-shaped cuts made in an edge or surface.

clue.text: Queen's secretary briefly confused by progressions

indicators.note: confused letters are muddled up and must be put into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped
SEC is the short form of secretary

explanation.surface: A royal secretary is bewildered by the course of events.
explanation.definitionFit: Sequences and progressions are both series of things following one another in order.

clue.text: Bet on run after deer

parts.note: an ante is a stake put up in poker
to lope is to run with long easy strides

explanation.surface: A gambler places a bet on a race after a deer has been spotted.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosely, an antelope is a deer-like grazing animal with horns; the clue treats them as kin.

clue.text: A month's endless credit is sterile

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: taken as written
SEP is the calendar abbreviation for September
buying on tick is buying on credit

explanation.surface: A month of unlimited credit leaves a shopper unable to produce anything.
explanation.walkthrough: On tick is informal British for on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: Aseptic means free of germs, which is what sterile means in a medical setting.

clue.text: Piece of furniture fit to model first

indicators.note: first tells the solver to put the piece for model at the front, before the other part

parts.note: the Model T was Ford's famous car
fit to do something means able to do it

explanation.surface: An item of furniture suitable for posing on first.
explanation.definitionFit: A table is a standard piece of household furniture, an example of the category named.

clue.text: Pink's not right, its kinky

parts.note: the opposite of right

indicators.note: kinky means twisted, so the short word before it is bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone frets that the colour pink is wrong and rather perverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Pink looks like a colour, but it is the political sense: mildly left-wing.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink is slang for mildly socialist, a paler shade of red, so a pink is a leftist.

clue.text: "Go out and have a ball": message from new poet (handwritten)

definitions.text: Go out and have a ball

indicators.note: making something new reshapes it, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: both words taken letter for letter, the brackets ignored

explanation.surface: A newly discovered poet's handwritten note urges the reader to go out and enjoy themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: To paint the town red is the idiom for a lively night out celebrating, partying hard.

clue.text: Magic of mist, say — swirling quite timelessly

indicators.note: say marks the word before it as a sound to be spelt another way

parts.note: the same sound with a y in place of the i

indicators.note: swirling things spin round, so the remaining letters are churned into a new order
without time means the letter standing for time is removed

parts.note: taken as written; time is T

explanation.surface: Swirling mist gives a scene a magical, almost timeless quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Mystique is an aura of mystery and glamour, a kind of magic surrounding a person or thing.

clue.text: Scientist gets away in a basket

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other, which holds it

parts.note: a wastepaper basket is a bin
off as in gone, away

explanation.surface: A scientist escapes hidden in a basket, like a stowaway.
explanation.walkthrough: Boffin is British slang for a scientist or technical expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Boffin is informal British slang for a research scientist or expert.

clue.text: Greeting heard from one after a drink or two

indicators.note: what is heard is only its sound, so the spelling may be different

parts.note: hi is a greeting, and the word sounds the same

explanation.surface: Someone a little tipsy calls out a cheery hello.
explanation.definitionFit: High is slang for intoxicated, the merry state a person may be in after a drink or two.

clue.text: Corrupt sexist term for fanatics

indicators.note: corrupt means spoilt or altered from the original, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A dodgy sexist expression used to describe zealots.
explanation.definitionFit: Extremists and fanatics are both people holding radical views pursued with excessive zeal.

clue.text: Neurotic put ham on bread in cooler, initially

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of each word in the run before it

parts.words: put ham on bread in cooler
parts.note: the leading letter of each of the six words

explanation.surface: A nervy person insists on chilling their ham sandwich in the fridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Phobic means having an irrational fear, a form of neurotic anxiety.

clue.text: Told swindlers about cat family

definitions.note: plural answer; the clue means members of the cat family

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so it is the sound of the word that matters

parts.note: swindlers are cheaters, which sounds the same in a non-rhotic accent

explanation.surface: Someone reports that conmen have been talking about a family of cats.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound-alike works in British speech, where the r of cheaters is not pronounced.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheetahs are big spotted cats, members of the feline family.

clue.text: Hide when per diem is lost

indicators.note: lost suggests the words have gone astray and must be found in a new arrangement

parts.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A worker hides away when their daily allowance is taken from them.
explanation.walkthrough: Hide looks like a verb, but it is the noun: an animal's skin. Per diem is a daily expenses allowance.
explanation.definitionFit: A hide is an animal's skin, and the epidermis is the outer layer of skin.

clue.text: Company's office promises energy for nothing

indicators.note: one thing for another means it takes the other's place in the word

parts.note: taken as written
E is the symbol for energy in physics
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A firm's head office pledges to supply power free of charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Premises are the building and land a business occupies, its office or site.

clue.text: Notes I'm compiling about damp

indicators.note: compiling means putting together, so the letters are assembled into a fresh order

parts.note: taken letter for letter, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone is writing up notes on dampness.
explanation.walkthrough: Damp looks like an adjective or noun, but it is the verb: to make wet.
explanation.definitionFit: To damp something is to make it slightly wet, which is to moisten it.

clue.text: Fixers for basic commodities

definitions.meaning: first meaning: wire clips that hold sheets of paper together
second meaning: the main foods or goods of everyday life

explanation.surface: Middlemen who arrange deals in essential goods.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both small metal paper fasteners and the essential items people buy regularly.

clue.text: Occupant is fashionable partner

parts.note: in means in fashion
a mate is a partner or spouse

explanation.surface: The person living there has a stylish other half.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is someone who occupies an institution such as a prison or hospital.

clue.text: Get rid of former student who can read

parts.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil of a school
one able to read is literate

explanation.surface: A school wants to be rid of an old pupil who has learned to read.
explanation.definitionFit: To obliterate something is to destroy it utterly, wiping it out completely.

clue.text: Deserves organ — new style, originally

parts.note: the ear is the organ of hearing
N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: originally points to how the word starts, so only its opening letter is kept

parts.note: the leading letter of the word

explanation.surface: A church organ deserves to be played in a fresh style.
explanation.definitionFit: To earn something is to merit or deserve it through one's efforts.

clue.text: Wife interrupted enthusiast, a young thing

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into the middle of something, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a fan is an enthusiast
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A wife cut into a fan's chatter about a young girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A fawn is a young deer, so it is literally a young thing; the vagueness is deliberate.

clue.text: Better penalty, right?

parts.note: a fine is a monetary penalty
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a punishment would be preferable.
explanation.definitionFit: Finer means of higher quality, which is what better means.

clue.text: Sporting dog for yours truly!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a gun dog breed trained to point at game
second meaning: the compiler of this very crossword, referring to themselves

explanation.walkthrough: Yours truly is how a writer refers to themselves; here the writer is the puzzle's compiler.
explanation.definitionFit: A setter is both a breed of gun dog and the person who composes a crossword.

clue.text: Guiding light for alumni working on railway

indicators.note: working means being worked on, so the letters are reshaped into another order

parts.note: taken as written
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Former students employed on the railway look to a beacon to guide them.
explanation.definitionFit: A luminary is an inspiring leader in a field, a guiding light to others.

clue.text: My angst's affected athletes

indicators.note: affected means changed or disturbed, so the letters are altered in order

parts.note: taken letter for letter, keeping the s

explanation.surface: A coach confesses that their anxiety has rubbed off on the sportspeople.
explanation.definitionFit: Gymnasts are athletes who compete in gymnastics, an example of the broader category.

clue.text: Walked out with half the street writing verse

indicators.note: half means only part of the word is kept and the rest is cut away

parts.note: taken as written
an ode is a piece of writing in verse

explanation.surface: A poet walked out, composing lines halfway down the road.
explanation.definitionFit: To stride is to walk with long steps, so strode is a past form of walking.
